title: Why Is DNS Now the Control Plane?
say: Welcome. This briefing is Book 08 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, DNS, DHCP and IPAM. It's about governing the name and address layer as one control plane, across the data center, every cloud and the branch edge. That may sound like plumbing, but here's the idea that drives the whole book. Every connection starts with a name. So whoever governs the name layer governs the enterprise. We'll go in four steps: why DNS is now the control plane, what has to change, who owns it, and how to migrate it and run it. Along the way you'll hear about failures that don't look like DNS failures at all, which is exactly why they're so hard to find. Let's start with why.

title: DNS now does six jobs it was never designed for
say: Almost every network connection begins with a DNS query. That's been true for a long time. What's changed is how much the answer now decides. In a hybrid, multi-cloud estate, DNS does six jobs its designers never planned for. For example, one storage name can answer privately inside its network and publicly everywhere else. DNS also picks which SaaS front door a user reaches, blocks known-bad domains before a connection is made, and carries certificate checks, because revocation endpoints are DNS names. The slide lists all six. NIST's 2026 guide puts it plainly: DNS has become more than a service; it's a security control. Yet many estates run it on as many as five platforms that share no state. The answer is one authoritative DDI policy plane, a requirement, not a product. Here's what goes wrong without one.

title: Split-brain DNS fails quietly, as something else
say: Run those platforms separately and you get split-brain DNS: the same name giving different answers depending on where the query starts. A designed split is fine. The problem is unplanned drift between systems with no shared state. Here's the classic case. A workload in AWS only gets an Azure private endpoint's private address through a forwarding rule. If that rule is missing or stale, the name still resolves, just to the public address. Microsoft attributes roughly seventy percent of private-endpoint access-denied cases to exactly that. The same drift happens with SaaS paths, and with security blocks that only apply on the resolver that answers. Either way, the failure is silent, and it shows up as something else. Changes come faster than any manual process can track. Only a control plane that holds the policy keeps everything in step. So what do the mandates actually require?

title: The mandates name no product, but describe one layer
say: The federal mandates never name a product, but read together they describe one governed name layer. It's worth being precise about who requires what. OMB requires encrypted DNS wherever it's supported, with endpoints pointed at designated resolvers. The requirement to send outbound resolution through Protective DNS comes from CISA's own guidance. The current logging memo, M-26-14, doesn't name DNS, but its logging and retention requirements land squarely on it. Other sources carry DNSSEC, and the latest TIC 3.0 catalog lists five DNS capabilities. The slide has the full list. NIST's March 2026 revision of its DNS deployment guide ties it together, but it's guidance, not a mandate. And FedRAMP certifies a cloud service, not an architecture, so the agency still authorizes its own DDI system. Now, the biggest thing that has to change: Active Directory.

title: Entra ID inherits none of what AD DNS does
say: For twenty years, Active Directory has been the hidden DNS service of the on-premises network. A domain's name becomes a zone, and every domain-joined machine points at the domain controllers for everything. Each domain controller registers the locator records clients use to find it, and secure dynamic updates keep them current. Entra ID inherits none of that. It hosts no zones and publishes no locator records. Yet hybrid-joined devices still go looking for a domain controller. So the plan is careful. The locator records stay where domain controllers can register them securely, either on AD DNS or a DDI platform that accepts secure updates, until the last domain controller goes. Everything else moves zone by zone, once it's been inventoried. But even a well-designed name layer only works if queries actually reach it.

title: Three ways a query escapes the governed path
say: Every control in the policy plane assumes the query reaches it. Three ordinary things decide whether it does, and none of them tells you when it doesn't. First, the branch edge. SD-WAN can redirect branch DNS to a designated resolver, but that target has to be a real agency resolver on the network, not an agent on the device itself. Second, encrypted DNS. Some forms can be blocked at the firewall except to approved resolvers. DNS over HTTPS hides inside normal web traffic, so it has to be governed on the endpoint, through browser and Windows policy. Third, rogue DHCP. One rogue server handing out its own resolver can move a whole subnet at once. AD authorization doesn't stop that; switch protections do. Next, a dependency that surprises people: certificates.

title: Every certificate check starts with a DNS lookup
say: A certificate can be valid, unrevoked and issued for the right name, and still fail. That's because every check that makes it trustworthy starts with a DNS lookup. Here's a real pattern. An agency's revocation list name exists only in AD DNS. A workload in AWS can't resolve it without a forwarding rule. The revocation check fails, a ticket gets opened against the PKI team, and the real cause can take days to find. DNSSEC is the other half. It proves where an answer came from and that it wasn't changed, but it doesn't encrypt anything. The program follows NIST. Always sign external zones and the dot-gov delegations. Validate on every agency resolver. Sign internal zones only where the system's authorization requires it. Validation stays on agency resolvers, because the cloud resolvers don't fully cover it. Next, the most common source of split-brain.

title: Forward the public zone to one point in Azure
say: Azure private endpoints are the most common source of private-address split-brain. When you create one, Azure writes its record into a private zone, and public DNS points into that name. You only get the private answer if your query reaches a resolver linked to that zone. So the rule is simple. Every origin, whether on-premises, another cloud or the branch, forwards the service's public zone to the Azure DNS Private Resolver. Not the private zone. And Azure Government uses different zone names, so commercial rules don't carry over. The Private Resolver is a bridge, not an authority, so you reach it by forwarding, never by delegation, and deploy one per region. Addresses need the same discipline, with the enterprise IPAM as the authority and the clouds reconciled against it. Put it together, and you get one governed path.

title: One governed path, five decisions that fail silently
say: Here's the whole path in one picture. A branch client's query goes from the SD-WAN edge to an agency resolver, then through the DDI policy plane, then to each cloud's private zones. Internet-bound lookups leave through CISA's Protective DNS. Five decisions carry almost all the operational risk. The edge points at a real agency resolver. That resolver is always the first hop. The policy plane holds every cloud forwarding rule. AD DNS is inventoried and rebuilt before any domain controller goes. And revocation endpoints resolve from everywhere. What makes these dangerous is that each one fails silently. The query still resolves, just outside policy or to the wrong address. So each decision comes with a check, run against the live configuration rather than the design document, before the next change. Which brings us to who owns all this.

title: Who decides, who does the work for DNS, DHCP and IPAM
say: In an AD estate, DNS belonged to whoever ran the domain controllers, and nobody really chose that. A single policy plane concentrates that authority, so its owners have to be named on purpose, with one decider per decision. The sponsor and CIO decide the platform model and when AD DNS and Windows DHCP retire. The CISO and ISSO set the requirements, like designated resolvers, DNSSEC and logging. The authorizing official accepts residual risk, including every standing exception. The DNS and DDI team runs the plane and decides what the edge points at. Network engineering configures it, and cloud teams consume it. Record changes come in three classes. Routine changes in a delegated namespace are pre-approved. Policy-driven records follow a change-controlled policy. And high-impact changes, like zones, delegations and forwarding, go to the change board. So how do we get there?

title: Six phases, one cutover loop, rollback at every step
say: The migration runs in six phases, from inventory and coexistence through to decommissioning AD DNS and DHCP, then hardening and evidence. Each phase ends with a rollback point and a resolution test from every origin, not a calendar date. Every move, whether it's a zone, a forwarder, a DHCP scope or a wave of clients, runs the same loop. Lower the time-to-live well ahead. Import with a dry run, never moving the core zone or locator records. Validate from everywhere. Then switch, and watch, while the old authority keeps answering. One warning from Azure: removing a network link deletes the records registered through it, and they can't be restored. And decommissioning is gated, never scheduled. The old servers retire only after the records resolve cleanly for a sustained period, parallel operation passes, and failover is tested. Then the plane has to run every day.

title: Operate it as one plane, and keep the evidence
say: One policy plane is only an improvement if divisions can still run their own networks through it. So each division gets a scope over its own zones, addresses and DHCP, with manager, operator and auditor roles. Automation is held to the same scopes. Infrastructure as code, ticketing workflows and certificate automation all go through one API and one audit trail. Locator records are checked from every site, every fifteen minutes, until the last domain controller retires. Drift reports compare the source of truth with every copy, and hygiene jobs catch stale and dangling records. The evidence floor is the federal logging memo. It doesn't name DNS, but its retention rules apply to it. Query logs, including encrypted queries, and DHCP lease history are how the name layer meets it. And lease history is what turns an address into a device. Now, choosing the platform.

title: Choose on evidence, price the meters, record the risk
say: Choose the platform on the evidence it produces for your own boundary, not on a brochure. Commercial DDI pricing is quoted per agency, so get every quote on the same assumptions. The cloud-native pieces have public prices and show up in every model. As one example, a hub with one inbound and one outbound Azure resolver endpoint costs about 362 dollars a month per region, and a second region doubles it. Remember that authorization belongs to a specific offering, not a vendor. The slide shows which DDI offerings have a FedRAMP authorization and which run inside the agency's own boundary. And a Moderate authorization doesn't cover GCC High or DoD. Some risk remains either way. Sync lag becomes the new source of divergence. A management outage blocks changes, though resolution keeps working. And encrypted DNS bypass stays possible where endpoint controls are incomplete. So, the decisions.

title: Decisions to make, and next steps
say: Here are the four decisions. First, authorize a single authoritative DDI policy plane and give it an owner, typically the enterprise architecture or network operations lead. Second, have that owner settle the five configuration decisions within ninety days, and report the residual risk to the authorizing official. Third, choose the platform on evidence: authorization at the right impact level, and quotes on the same assumptions. And fourth, name the owners, one decider per decision. The next step is Phase 1, the inventory. Export every AD DNS zone, locator record, forwarder and DHCP scope, every edge redirect target and every revocation endpoint, before anyone touches a domain controller. It's read-only, and it's the one step whose omission can't be repaired later. Govern the name layer as one plane, and it can carry the cloud, branch and identity transitions. Book 08 has the detail, every claim footnoted. Thank you.
